problem: Prior models on the SAIL maze-navigation dataset use bag-of-features perception that loses spatial relations (distance, order, relative position). SAIL is also small and unbalanced (3237 sentences, ~1/3 language-only), so a fixed test set cannot reliably tell models apart.
motivation: Instructions such as 'two alleys away from a sofa and a hatrack beyond that' need spatial perception. Small unbalanced data lets models be right for the wrong reasons; a blind language-only agent already gets 64% against ~70% for the state of the art. A controllable generator allows fair diagnosis of grounding ability.
key_idea: Represent the agent's view as an agent-centric grid that preserves spatial layout, feed it to a seq2seq model with a CNN using decoder-controlled channel attention, and compare models by learning efficiency on the controllable synthetic generator SAILx.
insight: The grid representation beats bag-of-features especially on spatially demanding tasks (Turn and Move to X 73.21 vs 64.29; Move to X 76.91 vs 73.21; overall 71.58 vs 69.54). On SAILx it needs fewer examples to reach 90% accuracy, and B.O.F fails to solve Any Combination within 250k instances. The language-only baseline scores 63.61 on SAIL, showing the dataset's bias and why fixed-size accuracy is a weak discriminator.
method: Grid perception: agent-centric grid with each row a direction (clockwise), first cell is the agent's location, first row copied to the last, 20 columns; each cell is a binary vector of item, floor and wall bits plus 3 cell-type bits (node, hall, non-walkable).
Encoder: bidirectional LSTM over one-hot words with embeddings; the final hidden state h = f_I ⊕ b_1 initializes the decoder.

Perceptual CNN with channel attention: first layer applies 1×m filters on the 5×20 grid; a softmax attention vector over channels is computed by a feedforward net from the decoder state s_{t-1}; further conv layers (2 for SAIL, 1 for SAILx) with relu and a final sigmoid.
Decoder: LSTM takes c_t ⊕ a_{t-1}; output o_t = W1 s_t + W2 c_t + b, softmax over {MOVE, LEFT, RIGHT, STOP}; trained with cross-entropy (teacher forcing) using Adam.
Inference: beam search, sentence by sentence for Paragraph while keeping the beam; ensembles average action distributions.

SAILx generator: 8x8 mazes via recursive backtracker, random items, floors and paintings, A* paths (start and goal at least 4 steps apart), task-pattern-specific text templates for the 8 task categories, controllable size and balance; a fixed 105k-instance release.
Evaluation protocol: six-fold cross-validation with each map split 50/50 into dev/test (avoids vTest and vDev issues); learning-efficiency metric = number of instances to reach 90% test accuracy.

setting.backbone: BiLSTM encoder + CNN with channel attention + LSTM decoder (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: SAIL Single-Sentence (3237 sentences, 3 maps); SAILx synthetic data (105k fixed set or streamed up to 250k) for the controlled experiments
setting.observation: symbolic agent-centric grid of items, floor patterns and wall paintings in line of sight
setting.action_space: discrete {MOVE, LEFT, RIGHT, STOP} on a maze graph
setting.simulator: SAIL maze environment and the custom SAILx generator
setting.privileged: none (symbolic perception is given as input)

numbers.extra: ensemble of 10; vTest-style comparison, but hyper-parameters tuned via 6-fold CV rather than per map
ensemble of 10; trained on single sentences; position match only

numbers.evidence: Table 'Results on the generated fixed data': Ours Test Ens. 93.48 (Avg. 91.82)

numbers_note: Learning-efficiency results (instances to reach 90%) are given only in a figure. Baseline comparison table (ensemble of 3): overall accuracy L.O. 63.61, B.O.F. 69.54, Ours 71.58.
results: The model reaches 72.82% on SAIL Single-Sentence with an ensemble of 10, beating Mei et al. (71.05, ens=10). On Paragraph it gets 32.57, comparable to Artzi et al. (35.44) which uses an extra lexicon. On SAILx, the grid model reaches 93.48 against 85.42 for bag-of-features.
limitations: Symbolic, fully specified grid perception in a tiny synthetic maze; not raw vision or realistic environments.
SAILx covers only part of the original language (very low coverage of Move Until and Any combination) and uses templated text without typos.
Paragraph performance is far below human (69.64), and the 90% learning-efficiency comparison covers only two models.
builds_on: Mei et al. 2015 (Listen, Attend, and Walk)
